findings.source_grounded_note: Hail, drought, winter freezing, grain deregulation, and shrinking household budgets interact. Industrial layoffs and lost cottage earnings reinforce hardship; machines and British imports attract blame, but treaty effects are qualified by their short time in force.

Popular celebrations mix royal loyalty with attacks on officials; troops still shoot crowds. Restoration includes cancellation of earlier reforms and expediting Estates-General, rather than a comprehensive new ministerial programme.

findings.topic: Forms of 1614 and collapse of anti-despotism unity
findings.source_grounded_note: Paris parlement intends to pre-empt manipulation, but separate chambers/votes expose privileged over-representation. The electoral-form dispute turns former patriotic heroes into suspected defenders of privilege.

Grenoble, Vizille, and Romans establish elective, doubled-third, common-voting principles under Mounier and Barnave. Their prior provincial experience supplies a national alternative and later political leadership.

findings.topic: Press freedom, clubs, and Society of Thirty
findings.source_grounded_note: Necker relaxes censorship and club restrictions. Duport’s predominantly noble group funds pamphlets/model petitions against privilege; municipal/literary networks build a movement that soon exceeds its organizers’ control.
The Essai frames privilege as parasitic and divisive, misleadingly associating it exclusively with nobles/clergy. Preserve author’s qualification alongside the argument’s mobilizing force.

Fear of being submerged drives refusal of doubled representation despite continued fiscal-equality commitment. Paris parlement’s narrow retreat and princes’ warnings deepen suspicion; the king rejects claims of noble loyalty.

findings.topic: Provincial representation and Necker’s unresolved voting rule
findings.source_grounded_note: Breton mass noble attendance and restrictive estates elsewhere cause inter- and intra-order conflict. December 27 doubles the third and allows cross-order election while leaving common voting to later agreement, embedding the central deadlock.

findings.topic: Third Estate as nation and patriotism
findings.source_grounded_note: Sieyès identifies the nation with associates under common law, excludes privileged orders, and advocates a unilateral national assembly. Patriot language shifts from opposition to despotism toward third-estate aspirations.
Third-estate refusal of business, noble intransigence, ignored royal suspension, and mobilized dependent crowds culminate in Rennes fighting. Bread-price demands complicate a simple two-class story.

Volney, Rabaut de Saint-Étienne, Robespierre, and local lawyers articulate grievances and organize meetings. Professional experience and accumulated resentment of privileged benches help explain their leadership.

Bailliages/sénéchaussées, grouped districts, city exceptions, Dauphiné/Navarre, and separate order assemblies matter. Broad male taxpayer primary participation leads through indirect selection; ecclesiastical corporations have delegates while beneficed priests attend.

findings.topic: Cahiers as mobilization and mediated evidence
findings.source_grounded_note: Village/corporate grievances are conflated and sometimes modeled, editing out poor people’s concerns. Nevertheless national consultation creates exceptional evidence and expands political expectations.

Rules favour parish priests, exclude incomplete ennoblements, and marginalize peasants/artisans without leisure. Third-estate deputies are largely legal/officeholding professionals rather than a merchant-led assembly; low participation qualifies expansive democratic language.

findings.topic: Popular unrest, Marseilles guard, and Réveillon riot
findings.source_grounded_note: Food/price action and authority failure lead electors at Marseilles to a patriotic guard. Réveillon’s cheap-bread remark is misread as wage cutting; destructive riots, repression, casualty rumours, and anti-rich cries unsettle incoming deputies.

findings.topic: Clerical reform demands and deeper confessional unity
findings.source_grounded_note: Parish-priest electoral victory seeks stipends, opportunity, and synods, yet clergy broadly want Catholic educational/censorial authority and limits on toleration. Later conflict should not erase this initial cross-rank unity.

Courtiers face resistance, robe elites lose heavily, Breton nobles boycott, and provincial families predominate. Fiscal equality unites more than voting rules; liberal/intransigent divisions cross social strata.

Status-coded dress and disappointing speeches reveal the contrast between hopes and ministerial equivocation. Separate verification threatens to settle voting by order before substantive business begins.

Breton/Dauphiné deputies insist on common verification; clergy seek compromise while nobles constitute separately. Failed talks, royal grief, Bailly’s presidency, and Sieyès’s final invitation precede the roll call.

findings.topic: Legality, audience pressure, and political reporting
findings.source_grounded_note: The third’s prolonged hesitation shows reluctance to breach law; unilateral verification begins revolutionary illegality. Spectators and Mirabeau’s reports reward firmness, while Palais Royal speech/print amplify opinion.

Priestly defections undermine order boundaries; the National Assembly title is followed by temporary tax authorization tied to its continued existence. This is a claim against royal authority as well as privileged chambers.

findings.topic: Tennis Court Oath and a misunderstood closure
findings.source_grounded_note: Locked doors for a Royal Session are read as impending dissolution; even previous moderates insist on continued meeting and a constitution. Clerical and noble accessions widen the Assembly.

The June 23 plan contains substantial reforms but reserves corporate vetoes, feudal property, royal approval, and exclusion of spectators. Its timing and threats defeat reconciliation; Mirabeau’s defiance and the king’s acquiescence collapse enforcement.

findings.topic: Popular pressure, soldiers, and union of orders
findings.source_grounded_note: Versailles crowds, threats to opponents, French Guards’ refusal, and expanding defections lead the king to order union on June 27. Deputies’ wish for calm differs from the popular movement’s continuing momentum.

Foreign regiments, Broglie’s command, and court attempts to reverse June gains sustain justified suspicion. The source infers intimidation/reversal as the purpose while explicitly leaving the new ministry’s precise intentions unclear.

findings.topic: Food crisis, toll-gates, and citizen militia
findings.source_grounded_note: Paris provisioning drains provincial markets; food riots help move clergy. Dismissal, cavalry action, armament, customs-wall destruction, and Saint-Lazare grain discovery prompt property owners to activate a militia unable initially to control crowds.

findings.topic: Bastille’s capture and French Guards’ expertise
findings.source_grounded_note: Arms from Invalides, failed negotiation, garrison fire, and defectors’ cannon explain surrender. The prison’s weak defences were not known beforehand; crowd initiative and military expertise both matter.

findings.topic: Unreliable coercion and end of royal authority
findings.source_grounded_note: Broglie fears wider indiscipline rather than shortage of soldiers. Withdrawal makes the king accept national sovereignty; Parisians see themselves as liberty’s guardians. The famous La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt exchange remains possibly apocryphal.

uncertainties.note: The precise programme of the Breteuil ministry is unclear; intimidation and reversal are the author’s inference from the military preparations.
The La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt remark is explicitly described as possibly apocryphal.

bindings.source_page_basis: one-based document pages and identical printed numeric labels

artifact_role: Source-first omission/readership notes only; not a canonical benchmark, typed editorial review, approval, or freeze.
